Regardless of my feelings against Monsanto, (and I do hate Monsanto) this article with its scary wording and link to the organizations own $100+ urine test seems more than a little disingenuous.

I followed links to the International Agency for Research on Cancer's study and it seems that Glyphosate is indeed a carcinogen best avoided.

Excerpt:

Glyphosate is a broad-spectrum herbicide, currently with the highest production volumes of all herbicides. It is used in more than 750 different products for agriculture, forestry, urban, and home applications. Its use has increased sharply with the development of genetically modified glyphosate-resistant crop varieties. Glyphosate has been detected in air during spraying, in water, and in food. There was limited evidence in humans for the carcinogenicity of glyphosate. Case-control studies of occupational exposure in the USA,14 Canada,6 and Sweden7 reported increased risks for non-Hodgkin lymphoma that persisted after adjustment for other pesticides. The AHS cohort did not show a significantly increased risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. In male CD-1 mice, glyphosate induced a positive trend in the incidence of a rare tumour, renal tubule carcinoma. A second study reported a positive trend for haemangiosarcoma in male mice.15 Glyphosate increased pancreatic islet-cell adenoma in male rats in two studies. A glyphosate formulation promoted skin tumours in an initiation-promotion study in mice.

Glyphosate has been detected in the blood and urine of agricultural workers, indicating absorption. Soil microbes degrade glyphosate to aminomethylphosphoric acid (AMPA). Blood AMPA detection after poisonings suggests intestinal microbial metabolism in humans. Glyphosate and glyphosate formulations induced DNA and chromosomal damage in mammals, and in human and animal cells in vitro. One study reported increases in blood markers of chromosomal damage (micronuclei) in residents of several communities after spraying of glyphosate formulations.16 Bacterial mutagenesis tests were negative. Glyphosate, glyphosate formulations, and AMPA induced oxidative stress in rodents and in vitro. The Working Group classified glyphosate as “probably carcinogenic to humans” (Group 2A).

That being said, isn't it more important to find how best to limit or avoid future exposure to Glyphosate rather than worry about to what degree you've already been exposed?

In the US it is now practically impossible to avoid heavy glyphosate exposure.

I think most people understand that things like corn in the US is predominately genetically modified and tends to contain heavy levels of glyphosate, but think they don't eat much of it so what's the big deal? The reality is that even corn alone is in nearly everything you eat. Look on the back of that softdrink you just downed and you'll see high fructose corn syrup. Other things containing that range from ketchup to fruit juice to yogurt and even salad dressing. Like fast food... anything? Most of all corporate fastfood "meat" uses corn as a filler to cut costs, fries are fried in vegetable oil which contains corn. Anything baked? Soup? Corn starch is there. Meat? Most of all livestock in the US is fed corn based feed. And that's just a small sampling of the foods with it in them.

And of course glyphosate has reached unprecedented levels of use in the US. As weeds grow somewhat ironically naturally resistant to it, farmers are left to pour more and more of the stuff on to get the job done. In 2012 159 million pounds of the stuff was poured on crops in just one year. And it's never cleaned up. It's left to sink into the ground which then pollutes the ground water. That ground water ends up being the stuff you drink, bathe in, and use and consume everyday.

In light of all of this Monsanto successfully lobbied the US government to increase the legal amount of allowable glyphosate residue on food. In fact, as mentioned in that article (from reuters), the US government no longer even regularly checks for levels of glyphosate on food citing as it's apparently "extremely expensive."
